newsitem.title: POLAND: President to fire controversial Polish army chief.
newsitem.headline: President to fire controversial Polish army chief.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski is to sack the armed forces Chief of Staff General Tadeusz Wilecki in a row over civilian control of the military.

Presidential spokesman Antoni Styrczula told Reuters on Monday: "The president will dismiss General Wilecki... and appoint General Henryk Szumski in his place." He said further details would be given at a news conference.

Critics have long accused Wilecki of seeking to entrench the general staff's authority at the expense of the defence ministry and of harming Poland's bid to fully meet exacting standards for civilian control of the armed forces required by NATO from aspiring new members.
With the Czech Republic and Hungary, Poland expects to be in the first wave of countries invited at NATO's July summit in Madrid to start talks on joining the alliance.

Wilecki's differences with the dominant party in the ruling coalition, Kwasniewski's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), exploded into an open row last week when the head of the party's parliamentary caucus said it was time for him to go.

Wilecki denies he has undermined civilian control of the military while arguing that he has provided vital stability of leadership and battled for adequate funds as the army prepared for NATO entry through years of changing governments and ministers.

"If anyone tries to change the leadership of the Polish army five minutes before the process of integration with NATO, I ask why?...I think one should not change the team at such a fraught moment," Wilecki told a public radio interviewer shortly before his dismissal was made known.
Wilecki's row with the SLD dates from late 1994 when general staff officers at a lunch in the Drawsko training ground were reported to have voted to remove the then defence minister.

Lech Walesa, Polish president at the time and sympathetic to army staff views, sacked the minister, arousing concerns in Poland and in NATO that parliamentary control of the military was not adequately established.
Last year, however, there was a major reform of Poland's command and control structures, entrenching the defence ministry's position.
Wilecki rejected arguments that he had undermined Poland's NATO case, saying that under his leadership, the military had drawn very close to the armies of the Western alliance.

"This is a very painful argument for us, because it is we who have brought Poland closer to NATO. Therefore it is hard to accuse us of obstructing the road to NATO entry," Wilecki told the radio interviewer.

He accused the SLD of reneging on earlier promises that it would bring spending on the military up to three percent of gross domestic product. He said it was still only at 2.3 percent, preventing vital modernisation and condemning army families to hardship.
"I have to say, with sadness, that certain obligations made above all by the left have not been honoured," he said.
Wilecki has received support over the past week from parts of the right-leaning opposition and from the Polish Peasant party (PSL), the SLD's smaller partner in the ruling coalition.
